One-line judgment: this line of work is not about pressing a start button, but about operating computer-controlled machine tools and equipment or robots to cut or form workpieces made of metal, plastics, wood, stone and other materials, and possibly taking on fixturing and equipment maintenance. O*NET defines the occupation as operating computer-controlled tools and machine tools or robots to machine or process parts and tools and other workpieces made of metal, plastic, wood, stone or other materials; may also be responsible for setting up and maintaining equipment; its tasks are led by measuring finished parts to confirm they meet specifications and setting up and operating computer-controlled machine tools or robots to complete one or more machining operations, and this page is developed on the precise occupational scope of O*NET-SOC 51-9161.00.

Signals for continuing to explore: you are willing to check step by step against drawings and program specifications, judge tool and equipment condition with feel and sound and gauge readings, and stop, record, and then decide whether to continue or escalate when dimensions drift or anomalies appear. O*NET work context shows 99% wear common protective or safety equipment every day, 81% consider being very exact or highly accurate extremely important (17% very important), 77% stand continuously or almost continuously (13% about half the time), 62% face strict deadlines every day (23% once a week or more), 65% continuously or almost continuously use hands to handle objects and tools (21% about half the time), 60% are exposed to hazardous equipment every day (12% never), 53% come into contact with contaminants every day (11% once a month or more), 52% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day, 51% are in continuous contact with others (16% most of the time), 48% make decisions every day that affect others or financial resources or organizational reputation, 45% consider repetitive tasks extremely important (23% very important), 44% consider it extremely important that work pace is completely determined by equipment speed (34% very important), 39% have a lot of decision freedom (38% some freedom), and 50% work more than 40 hours per week (49% work 40 hours).

Conditions for pausing before high investment: you have not yet gone through a complete loop of reading drawings and program specifications — fixturing and alignment — trial cut and first-article measurement — judging from dimensions whether to continue — anomaly stop and recording and escalation, in a simulation or paper process, nor have you checked the employer rules on machine tool operating authorization, guarding and safety devices, first-article confirmation and measurement records, and cutting fluid and chip handling. The preparation level for this occupation is Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation needed), the education distribution wording on that page is that a high school diploma or equivalent is usually required and some positions do not require it, and the SVP range is less than 6.0; that page also provides 2 national certifications (Machining Level I - CNC Milling: Programming Setup & Operations, ISA Certified Control Systems Technician - Level I), but certification does not equal operating authorization or first-article release authority, and this page does not infer an individual hiring probability from them.

Education, job training, professional certification, licenses and position authority must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation needed), the education distribution wording on that page is that a high school diploma or equivalent is usually required and some positions do not require it, and the SVP range is less than 6.0; that page also provides 2 national certifications (Machining Level I - CNC Milling: Programming Setup & Operations, ISA Certified Control Systems Technician - Level I); but certification does not equal a degree, an employer appointment, machine tool operating authorization, first-article release or sign-off authority; machine tool and robot operating authorization, guarding and safety devices and lockout/tagout, and the requirements involving cutting fluid and chips and waste handling must be confirmed item by item against the applicable jurisdiction and employer systems, and may involve the rules of the occupational safety and health authorities; this page explains tasks and boundaries based on O*NET and public sources and does not present education or certification as a statutory qualification.

One line: this is an occupation in which reading accurately, setting up steadily and measuring clearly are all indispensable; whether the first article can be made right the first time, whether tools can be changed in time, and whether an out-of-tolerance dimension can be found before a whole batch is scrapped determine whether your output is trusted. If you are willing to speak with drawings and gauges and records rather than gambling on feel, it deserves serious consideration.

The work of numerically controlled machine tool operators can be divided into three linked but independent work dimensions. The first is fixturing and program preparation: read program specifications or drawings to determine and set machine operation and machining sequence and finished dimensions and numerical control sequence; use tools and precision measuring instruments to install and align and tighten tools and attachments and fixtures and workpieces; calculate machine speeds and feed ratios and cutting dimensions and positions; modify machine programs on the computer and enter new specification parameters; transmit commands from the server to the numerical control module over a computer network link; insert control instructions into the machine control unit to start machining; enter initial part dimensions into the machine control panel; write simple programs; and prepare fixturing for subsequent tasks while the machine is running. The second is machining operation and equipment maintenance: set up and operate computer-controlled machine tools or robots to complete machining operations; listen to machine running sounds to identify problems such as dull tools or excessive vibration and adjust the machine; monitor machine operation and panel displays and compare readings with specifications to find faults; adjust feed and speed or change tools or adjust controls when automatic programming fails or the machine breaks down; stop the machine to remove finished parts or change tools and fixtures and workpieces; check and ensure the workpiece is properly lubricated and cooled during machining; control the coolant system; maintain the machine tool and use hand tools to remove and replace broken or worn machine-tool tooling; modify cutting programs to deal with problems encountered during machining and save the modified programs; and clean the machine tool and tools and parts. The third is dimensional inspection and recording and collaboration: use precision measuring instruments and templates and fixtures to measure finished part dimensions to confirm they meet specifications; communicate with supervisors or programmers to resolve machine tool faults or production errors or to obtain approval to continue production; stack or load finished parts or place parts onto conveyor systems; and mark shot peening areas and load shot, or inspect electronic components under a microscope for defects or integrity after laser trimming.

Fixturing and program preparation: read drawings and program specifications, fixture and align tools and fixtures and workpieces, calculate speed and feed and cutting dimensions, modify and enter programs and transmit them to the numerical control module

Read drawings and program specifications → fixture and align tools and fixtures and workpieces → enter initial dimensions and parameters → trial cut and measure the first article → judge from dimensions and appearance whether to continue → archive first-article and fixturing records

Machining operation and equipment maintenance: operate machine tools and robots, listen and monitor panel readings, adjust feed and speed and tools, maintain and replace worn parts, control coolant, clean and service

Confirm the program and fixturing → start and listen to the machine and watch panel readings → adjust feed and tools on anomalies → stop to change tools or fixtures → check lubrication and cooling → service and clean and write the shift handover record

Dimensional inspection and recording and collaboration: use precision measuring instruments and templates and fixtures to measure finished part dimensions, judge pass or fail against specifications, communicate anomalies with supervisors or programmers, load and stack finished parts, and record measurement and anomaly and handover information.

There is overlap with machinist / programming, equipment repair and assembly roles. This occupation can fixture, modify and write simple programs, and the final responsibility for process planning and complex programming must be checked against the organization and is not ruled out wholesale. Materials also include plastic / wood / stone, so the whole occupation cannot be defined only by metal cutting.

Make workpieces according to drawings and specifications: turn drawing and program requirements into executable fixturing and cutting, and hold dimensions and surface quality in the first article and batch production

Operate numerically controlled machine tools and equipment or robots: fixture and align tools and workpieces, set parameters and modify programs, listen and monitor operation, measure dimensions and handle anomalies

Advance the work based on the O*NET occupational definition and 27 tasks, drawings and program specifications and process cards, measured data from precision measuring instruments and templates and fixtures, and the employer systems for machine tool operating authorization and guarding and safety and cutting fluid management

This occupation takes machining execution and self-inspection under an established program as its object; machinist and machine tool programming roles take process plans and program development and tolerance decisions as their object

Editorial cycle example: read the drawing → fixture → verify parameters → trial run / first article per machine model procedure → compare with specifications → record; this does not replace the machine model safety procedure or employer approval.

Industrial machinery mechanics focus on equipment fault diagnosis and repair; this occupation treats routine machine tool maintenance and worn part replacement as part of machining execution, and stops and reports when an equipment anomaly exceeds its own handling scope

First-article measurement and patrol inspection records, tool and fixture and workpiece fixturing records, program modification and parameter and tool offset records, equipment inspection and maintenance and worn part replacement records, anomaly and stop and escalation records, output and handover records

Electromechanical assembly focuses on components and assemblies, while this occupation focuses on computer-controlled machine tool / robot machining; duties may overlap, and the specific cutting and adjustment boundary is checked against the position.

Editorial principle: dimensions and safety come first, fixturing / operation / maintenance are carried out according to the machine model and actual authorization, and the basis for measurements and changes is retained. U.S. OSHA1910.212 requires guarding of applicable machine hazard points; 1910.147 applies to servicing and maintenance with risk of injury from unexpected startup or release of stored energy, with conditional exceptions for normal production and minor tasks. Buttons / control switches are not energy isolation devices. Specific tasks are carried out by authorized trained personnel according to the machine model and organizational procedures, and U.S. rules are not written as China statutory qualifications.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether drawings and program specifications are read to an executable level; whether fixturing and alignment are solid and reliable; whether the first article is measured and judged against specifications; whether tools and coolant and worn parts are checked and replaced on schedule; whether anomalies are handled according to the stop and record and escalation process; and whether fixturing and measurement and program modifications are recorded traceably.
Judgment one: whether drawings and program specifications are read to an executable level

Turn drawing dimensions and tolerances and surface requirements and program specifications into executable fixturing and cutting steps (datum and alignment and tool position and speed and feed and depth of cut); confirm unclear points in the drawing or program before starting; do not replace verification with groundless wording such as just follow it.
Judgment two: whether fixturing and alignment are solid and reliable

Choose a suitable fixturing method according to the workpiece and fixture and tool and align and tighten it; confirm that the locating datum and machining allowance and clamping force will not cause deformation; use auxiliary support or multiple passes for easily deformed parts such as thin walls and long overhangs.
Judgment three: whether the first article is measured and judged against specifications

Measure key dimensions of the first article with precision measuring instruments and templates and judge pass or fail against specifications; analyze the cause of out-of-tolerance parts (tool wear and tool offset and thermal deformation and fixturing) before deciding on adjustments; archive first-article and setup records and confirm the state is stable before batch production.
Judgment four: whether tools and coolant and worn parts are checked and replaced on schedule

Decide the replacement time according to tool life and wear and judgment based on operating sounds and record it; confirm lubrication and cooling are in place and the coolant concentration and flow are normal; remove and replace broken or failed machine-tool tooling according to maintenance requirements.
Judgment five: whether anomalies are handled according to the stop and record and escalation process

Stop the machine and preserve on-site information first when abnormal noise or alarms or sudden dimension changes occur; handle it yourself within the scope of authority or report to a supervisor or programmer; do not bypass guarding and safety devices on your own initiative or continue machining with a fault.
Judgment six: whether fixturing and measurement and program modifications are recorded traceably

Record the fixturing method and alignment results and parameters and tool offsets and program modification dates and reasons and measurement results; let the colleague taking over judge the equipment and workpiece state from the records; distill recurring deviations into a reusable adjustment checklist.

The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: reading drawings and tolerances, reading equipment condition, operating and inspecting according to procedures, and keeping measurement and anomaly records. The real difference lies in the scope of responsibility: this occupation focuses on operating numerically controlled machine tools according to an established program to complete machining and self-inspection; the robotics direction focuses on system integration and commissioning; the equipment repair direction focuses on fault diagnosis and repair; the machinist direction focuses on process plans and programs and tolerance decisions; the electromechanical and electrical assembly direction focuses on component and assembly assembly; the aviation assembly direction focuses on structural parts and systems assembly and rigging. When choosing, it is suggested to first verify with a deliverable exercise of reading drawings — fixturing — trial cut and first-article measurement — judgment and recording, rather than comparing titles first.

The comparison is based on the occupational definition and 27 tasks and work activities and work context descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 51-9161.00 page, the related and adjacent occupation codes listed there, the adjacent occupation slug list registered in this evidence route (robotics-technicians, industrial-machinery-mechanics, aircraft-structure-surfaces-rigging-and-systems-assemblers, electrical-and-electronic-equipment-assemblers, electromechanical-equipment-assemblers), and public occupational materials for each adjacent occupation; the comparison is editorial synthesis and does not constitute an occupational safety, environmental or legal conclusion.

The table below compares roles and occupations adjacent to this occupation: robotics technicians, industrial machinery mechanics, machinists, electromechanical equipment assemblers, electrical and electronic equipment assemblers, and aircraft structure and surfaces and rigging and systems assemblers. The four columns each answer the same kind of question: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

Robotics technicians focus on the assembly and commissioning and integration and maintenance of robotic systems and usually do not carry batch cutting operations; this occupation focuses on operating numerically controlled machine tools to complete machining and self-inspection.
People willing to do system integration and commissioning and maintenance suit that direction; people willing to do machining execution and dimensional control suit this occupation.
Mainly commissioning and integration and maintenance records.
Robotics technicians

Industrial machinery mechanics focus on fault diagnosis and repair and preventive maintenance of industrial machinery and usually do not carry machining execution; this occupation treats routine equipment maintenance and worn part replacement as part of machining execution.
People willing to do equipment diagnosis and repair suit that direction; people willing to do machine tool operation and first-article confirmation suit this occupation.
Mainly fault diagnosis and repair and inspection records.
Industrial machinery mechanics

Machinists focus on the machining process and tool and tolerance control of manual and numerically controlled machine tools and usually carry more complex process decisions and program writing; this occupation focuses on executing an established program and self-inspecting.
People willing to do process plans and program writing and tolerance decisions suit that direction; people willing to do fixturing and operation and measurement suit this occupation.
Mainly process plans and programs and inspection records.
Machinists

Electromechanical equipment assemblers focus on the assembly and adjustment of electromechanical components and assemblies and do not involve cutting and forming; this occupation takes cutting operations and dimensional control as its object.
People willing to do component and assembly assembly suit that direction; people willing to do machine tool operation and cooling and tool maintenance suit this occupation.
Mainly assembly and adjustment and test records.
Electromechanical equipment assemblers

Electrical and electronic equipment assemblers focus on the assembly of electrical and electronic components and harnesses and assemblies and do not involve machine tool cutting and process parameters; this occupation takes machining and equipment operation and maintenance as its object.
People willing to do electrical and electronic assembly suit that direction; people willing to do machining and equipment maintenance suit this occupation.
Mainly assembly and wiring and test records.
Electrical and electronic equipment assemblers

Aircraft structure and surfaces and rigging and systems assemblers focus on the assembly and rigging of aircraft structural parts and systems and usually do not carry general mechanical cutting operations; this occupation takes numerically controlled cutting and dimensional inspection as its object.
People willing to do aviation assembly and rigging suit that direction; people willing to do numerically controlled machining and gauge inspection suit this occupation.
Mainly assembly and rigging and inspection records.
Aircraft structure and surfaces and rigging and systems assemblers

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires adding new capabilities and experience: the robotics direction needs robot programming and integration and commissioning experience; the machinery repair direction needs fault diagnosis and repair and preventive maintenance experience; the machinist direction needs process plans and program writing and tolerance analysis experience; the electromechanical assembly direction needs component and assembly assembly and testing experience; the electrical assembly direction needs electrical and electronic assembly and wiring and testing experience; the aviation assembly direction needs structural part assembly and rigging and inspection experience. Drawing reading and gauges and equipment operation capabilities can transfer, but the scope of responsibility and authority of each direction must be re-established.

The five steps below are the editorial process given on this page, used to explain who is responsible at which step; they are not a mandatory process prescribed by a source, nor do they replace the employer's own machine tool operation and guarding and safety and quality management systems.

Clarify the drawings and program specifications and batch requirements and your own operating authorization boundary, as well as your decision scope for first-article confirmation and parameter adjustment and stop escalation.

In tools that the organization permits and that have been tested, trial annotations, conversions and checklists / records, check versions and sources, and do not enter candidate parameters directly into a real machine.

Reviewed by yourself and the reviewers: whether the datum and alignment and clamping are stable, whether the first-article dimensions and appearance are acceptable, and whether tool offset and parameter changes meet the process requirements.

Keep fixturing and parameters and tool offsets and program modifications and measurements and anomalies and stops and handovers on record; keep gauge numbers and calibration status and raw readings according to quality requirements.

Roles with the corresponding authority and qualifications confirm machine tool operating authorization and safety and quality conclusions; tools do not carry that responsibility and do not exempt anyone from occupational safety and environmental obligations.

Automatically generated cutting parameters or tool offset suggestions may not match the machine and tool and material and fixturing state; entering them without confirmation may cause tool breakage and scrapped workpieces and even equipment damage.

Editorial suggestion: check the output against the machine model manual, the process and the approved program; validation is carried out by trained authorized personnel under the specified protection conditions, and dry running / single block does not prove that all collision and cutting risks have been ruled out, and the fictional exercise does not start a real machine.
Drawings and programs and process parameters are protected information, and uploading them to external services may cause technical information leakage and compliance risk.

Choose usable tools and deployment methods according to information classification and authorization, desensitize identifiable information or use controlled systems, and keep access and export records.
Programs or parameters generated by tools that are run automatically without review and trial-cut validation bypass first-article confirmation and cannot be traced back when a tool collision occurs.
Make program review and dry running and first-article confirmation fixed human preconditions; tools are used only for generation and conversion, with program and parameter version records kept.
Using automatically grouped alarms or trends to determine equipment state directly may mask early signs such as mechanical wear and gradual tool degradation and loose fixturing.
Combine sound and feel with measurements and inspection records, mark the applicable scope of conclusions and keep the raw data, and have equipment state conclusions confirmed by review.
When the process is split into tools giving parameters and humans clicking confirm, a gap easily appears where no one is responsible for first-article acceptability and equipment safety.

paragraphs: The six cards are editorial scenarios and control suggestions derived from the tasks, not incident rates / rankings / a uniform employer system. The original U.S. machine guarding and energy control texts are listed separately; specific machine model / organizational safety and hazardous chemical systems for China were not obtained, so check against the actually applicable rules.

The editorial suggestion is to check fixturing / alignment, tool cooling, program tool offsets, measurement and handover, protection and energy control first; possible consequences include displacement, out-of-tolerance, damage and personal risk, and no ranking of what is most needed or most common is given.

Occupational tasks and the U.S. context come from O*NET51-9161; 2025 wages and 2025—2035 employment are kept separate, and the precise China gap and the manufacturing background are labeled separately. U.S. OSHA1910.212 requires guarding of applicable machine hazard points; 1910.147 applies to servicing and maintenance with risk of injury from unexpected startup or release of stored energy, with conditional exceptions for normal production and minor tasks. Buttons / control switches are not energy isolation devices. Specific tasks are carried out by authorized trained personnel according to the machine model and organizational procedures, and U.S. rules are not written as China statutory qualifications.
Roles that carry fixturing and alignment responsibility

Unreliable fixturing and alignment or improper clamping force can cause the workpiece to shift or fly out or the tool to collide during cutting, and affect dimensional acceptability and personal safety.

Choose the locating datum and fixture and clamping method according to the drawing and process and align and confirm them; use auxiliary support or multiple passes for thin-walled and overhanging parts; confirm the tool and fixture and workpiece are tightened before starting and keep fixturing records.
Skipping alignment based on experience; using non-compliant shims or temporary fixtures; going straight to automatic operation without dry running or single block validation to save time.
Roles that carry tool and cooling and equipment maintenance responsibility
Tool wear or breakage not replaced in time and inadequate cooling and lubrication will cause dimensional drift and worse surface quality, and may damage the spindle and machine tool.

Decide the replacement time according to tool life and wear and sound judgment and record it; confirm coolant concentration and flow and adequate lubrication; check the machine against the inspection checklist and replace broken or worn parts and keep records.
Using a tool until it chips before changing it; never testing or changing the coolant; signing off the inspection checklist without actually checking.
Roles that carry safety and protection responsibility

Failed or bypassed guard doors and interlocks and emergency stops, and non-compliant handling of hazardous chemicals and chips and waste, will cause personal injury and compliance and environmental liability.

Applicable U.S. machine hazard points must have effective guarding; when servicing and maintenance involve unexpected startup or stored energy risk, isolate and verify according to the 1910.147 procedure. An ordinary stop button is not an isolation device. Whether tool changes / cleaning fall under it must be checked against the specific procedure and regulatory conditions, and exceptions are not applied on your own initiative; China conditions are checked separately.
Removing or shorting guards and interlocks for easier observation; clearing chips with bare hands; discharging cutting fluid and waste oil straight into the drain.
Roles that carry program and tool offset modification
Program or tool offset changes that are unconfirmed or unversioned cannot be traced back after a shift change or part change, and cause batch out-of-tolerance or tool collision.

Editorial suggestion: keep versions, reasons and personnel for program / tool offset changes according to actual authority; carry out validation according to the machine model / approved process program, where dry running / single block does not prove all risks are ruled out, and have release confirmed by actually authorized personnel.
Changing tool offsets on the fly without reporting; restoring the original number from memory; several people sharing the same program version without leaving modification traces.
Roles that carry dimensional measurement and recording responsibility
Uncalibrated gauges or improper measurement methods or wrong reading records will pass out-of-tolerance parts as acceptable into the next process, causing rework and scrapping and customer claims.

Check gauge numbers and calibration status according to quality requirements and measure according to the procedure; record raw readings and measurement positions and environmental conditions; isolate and identify and report out-of-tolerance parts according to the nonconforming product process.
Estimating by habit instead of using gauges; not sending gauges for calibration when due; mixing out-of-tolerance parts together before deciding what to do.
Roles that carry changeover and handover responsibility
Changeover and handover that do not synchronize equipment and program and tool state will cause the next shift's first article to fail or the equipment to run with a fault.

Write the equipment state and work in progress and program version and tool and coolant state into the handover record; specify the responsible person and next step for unfinished items; distill recurring problems into a handling checklist and track corrective actions.
Explaining things only verbally; copying the previous shift's content into the handover sheet; handing over faulty equipment without identification.

values: Fictional task: in a simulation or paper process, complete the fixturing and parameter setting and trial cut and first-article measurement of a fictional part, and write the fixturing and alignment plan and parameters and tool offsets and first-article judgment and anomaly handling and records.

Fictional materials: a fictional part drawing (including key dimensions and tolerances and surface requirements and one unclear datum marking), a fictional program specification, and a fictional blank dimension and material description.
Fictional conditions: a fictional list of available machines and tools and fixtures, and a fictional protection and lockout/tagout and cutting fluid handling requirement.
Fictional constraints: a fictional limit on batch size and delivery date and available hours and quality inspection sampling ratio.

Step one: write out drawing reading and process understanding (list the key dimensions and tolerances and datum and machining allowance and the points that need confirmation from programming or process staff).

Step two: write out the fixturing and alignment and parameter plan (locating and clamping method and alignment method and speed and feed and depth of cut and tool offset settings, explaining the trade-off rationale), and explain which steps need dry running or single block validation.

Step three: write out the first-article measurement and judgment and anomaly handling and recording plan (including measurement items and gauges and criteria and out-of-tolerance analysis path and stopping and escalation conditions and record elements), and explain which decisions must be confirmed by operating authorization or process or quality inspection roles.

Reference deliverables: a drawing reading and process understanding checklist, a fixturing and alignment and parameter plan, and a first-article measurement and judgment and anomaly handling and recording plan.

Evaluation basis: whether key dimensions and tolerances are identified, whether fixturing and alignment are solid and feasible, whether parameters and tool offsets have a basis, whether first-article criteria are executable, whether the out-of-tolerance analysis path is reasonable, whether stopping and escalation conditions are clear, whether records are traceable, and whether changes beyond authority are identified as requiring authorized confirmation.
Multiple reasonable approaches are allowed; if some information is judged insufficient, explicitly state which parts are insufficient and what additional information is needed.

All materials in this exercise are fictional and must not be trial cut on a real machine, must not use real drawings or programs, and must not serve as a basis for operating authorization or quality release or safety decisions; real machining must follow the applicable jurisdiction and employer systems and be carried out by roles with the corresponding authority and qualifications.
The machines and tools and fixtures and batch size given in the prompt are all fictional values, used only to practice fixturing and first-article and recording thinking.

A table: break each role requirement (education and professional foundation, machining or CNC operating practical experience, training or vocational skill level or certification, machine tool and robot operating authorization, guarding and safety devices and lockout/tagout requirements, cutting fluid and chip and waste and hazardous chemical management requirements) into 'condition - demonstrable experience - evidence location' line by line.

Evidence forms include desensitized fixturing and parameter and tool offset and program modification and first-article and patrol inspection records and out-of-tolerance handling records, and training and authorization records.

entries.answer: Daily work centers on fixturing and program preparation, machining operation and equipment maintenance, and dimensional inspection and recording and collaboration: read drawings and program specifications and set operation and sequence and dimensions; use tools and precision measuring instruments to install and align and tighten tools and fixtures and workpieces; calculate machine speed and feed and cutting dimensions and modify and enter programs; set up and operate the machine or robot and monitor operation by sound and gauges; adjust feed and speed or change tools or adjust controls on anomalies; stop the machine to remove finished parts or change tools and fixtures; check lubrication and cooling and maintain and replace worn parts; measure finished part dimensions with precision gauges and judge against specifications; communicate anomalies with supervisors or programmers; and load finished parts and record and hand over. The work context shown on this page: 99% wear common protective or safety equipment every day, 81% consider being very exact or highly accurate extremely important, and 77% stand continuously or almost continuously.
entries.question: What does a numerically controlled machine tool operator do every day?

entries.answer: Robotics technicians focus on the assembly and commissioning and integration and maintenance of robotic systems; industrial machinery mechanics focus on fault diagnosis and repair and preventive maintenance of industrial machinery; machinists focus on process plans and program writing and tolerance control and carry more complex process decisions; electromechanical equipment assemblers focus on component and assembly assembly and adjustment; electrical and electronic equipment assemblers focus on electrical and electronic assembly and wiring and testing; aircraft structure and surfaces and rigging and systems assemblers focus on aviation structural part and system assembly and rigging. This occupation focuses on operating numerically controlled machine tools to complete machining and self-inspection according to drawings and programs, and usually does not carry final responsibility for process design and program development. Shared capabilities do not mean the roles are interchangeable: the scope of responsibility and the authority differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between this occupation and adjacent occupations?

entries.answer: It cannot be inferred that way. The core tasks of this occupation include fixturing and alignment judgment, abnormal sound and vibration identification and on-site adjustment, first-article acceptability judgment, and stop and escalation decisions; these steps depend on on-site feel and experience and authority and responsibility. In addition, the ILO exposure index registered in this evidence route is only a task exposure measure, not a replacement rate or job reduction forecast. The more reliable uses of tools are program annotation and parameter conversion and checklists and record drafts. Note also that the BLS projection on this occupation's page shows an 11% employment decline for 2024—2034 (Decline), which is a national projection containing assumptions and error and does not equal an individual hiring probability.

The later-affected parts are the steps requiring feel and judgment and responsibility: datum and alignment and clamping judgment, abnormal sound and vibration identification and on-site adjustment, first-article acceptability judgment and stop and escalation decisions. It must be stressed that this judgment is editorial synthesis, not an exposure measure or job forecast provided by a source.

description.text: Numerically controlled machine tool operators operate computer-controlled machine tools and robots to machine workpieces made of metal and plastic and other materials, centered on fixturing and program preparation, machining operation and equipment maintenance, and dimensional inspection and recording and collaboration: 27 tasks and the work context, the U.S. 2025 median wage of 50,690 USD and 2024—2034 decline of 11%, the Mainland China occupation-level wage gap and the boundary of publishing no values, and entry and qualifications and operating authorization and safety boundaries and the exercise, all in one view.

subject.name: Numerically controlled machine tool operator
subject.summary: Operate computer-controlled tools and machine tools or robots to machine or process parts and tools and other workpieces made of metal, plastic, wood, stone or other materials, and possibly be responsible for fixturing and maintaining equipment: read drawings and program specifications and set operation and sequence and dimensions; install and align and tighten tools and attachments and fixtures and workpieces; calculate machine speed and feed and cutting dimensions and modify and enter programs; set up and operate the machine or robot and listen and monitor operation; adjust feed and speed or change tools on anomalies; check lubrication and cooling and maintain and replace worn parts; measure finished part dimensions with precision gauges and compare against specifications; communicate anomalies with supervisors or programmers; and load finished parts and record and hand over.
